title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: which past does the sentence need?

questions.prompt: Complete: "The technicians ___ come back from the site, so you can have the report today."

options.text: were already
have already
have yet
has already

questions.explanation: "have already" is the pair the sentence needs: already stands between the auxiliary and the participle, and the plural subject The technicians takes have — the technicians have already come back. "has already" hands a plural subject a singular auxiliary. "have yet" puts yet in an affirmative sentence, where English uses already; yet belongs to negatives and questions, at the very end. "were already" builds the present perfect on be, but the present perfect is always have or has plus the participle.

questions.prompt: Only one of these sentences is correct English. Which one?

options.text: Sami has gone back to his old job.
Sami have gone back to his old job.
Sami has goed back to his old job.
Sami has went back to his old job.

questions.explanation: "Sami has gone back to his old job." is the correct one: the present perfect is has plus the third form of go, which is gone, and no moment is named. "Sami have gone back to his old job." gives a singular subject the plural auxiliary. "Sami has goed back to his old job." invents a regular -ed form for a verb that is irregular. "Sami has went back to his old job." puts the simple past went after has, where only the participle gone can stand. The classic mistake is exactly that: column two of the table instead of column three.

options.text: The gallery has already answered our email yet.
The gallery has yet answered our email.
The gallery hasn't answered our email yet.
The gallery hasn't answered yet our email.

questions.explanation: "The gallery hasn't answered our email yet." is right: yet stands at the very end of the sentence, and only in a negative or a question. "The gallery has already answered our email yet." and "The gallery has yet answered our email." are affirmative, where yet has no place at all — an affirmative takes already, between has and the participle. "The gallery hasn't answered yet our email." separates the participle from its object, which English does not allow. The trap here is to treat yet as a middle-of-the-sentence adverb like already.

questions.prompt: Read: "The repair workshop has trained forty apprentices." Which analysis of the tense is correct?

options.text: Present perfect, because no time is stated.
Present perfect, because the training happened long ago.
Present simple, because it is a general truth.
Simple past, because the action is over.

questions.explanation: "Present perfect, because no time is stated." is the right reading: has trained gives the score today and never says when. "Present perfect, because the training happened long ago." keeps the tense but invents a moment the sentence never gives. "Simple past, because the action is over." would need a stated moment such as last year, and the form here is has trained, not trained. "Present simple, because it is a general truth." ignores that form completely. The classic mistake is to believe the present perfect is the tense of distant or dated events.

questions.prompt: Read this text, then answer. "(1) Mehdi opened a small bicycle garage in Menzel Bourguiba in 2012. (2) He bought his first set of tools with the money from a summer job. (3) Two winters ago the river flooded the street and he lost everything in one night. (4) Since that flood he made the garage bigger than before, and he has never lost a customer." Which sentence uses the wrong tense?

options.text: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4

questions.explanation: Sentence 4 is the faulty one: "Since that flood" gives a starting point that reaches today, and a starting point never takes a simple past — Since that flood he has made the garage bigger than before ✓. Sentences 1 and 2 are dated by in 2012, so opened and bought belong to the simple past. Sentence 3 is dated by two winters ago, so flooded and lost belong to the simple past too. The second half of sentence 4 is already right: he has never lost a customer names no moment, and never sits between has and the participle.

questions.prompt: Turn this sentence into a question without changing the tense: "Yosra has left the old supplier."

options.text: Did Yosra leave the old supplier?
Has Yosra leave the old supplier?
Has Yosra left the old supplier?
Have Yosra left the old supplier?

questions.explanation: "Has Yosra left the old supplier?" keeps the present perfect: the question moves has in front of the subject and keeps the participle left untouched. "Did Yosra leave the old supplier?" is a well-formed sentence, but it switches to the simple past, which the instruction forbids. "Has Yosra leave the old supplier?" replaces the participle with the base form, and "Have Yosra left the old supplier?" gives a singular subject the plural auxiliary. What catches most students is changing the tense while turning a statement into a question.
